title: The bids are in, the winners aren't picked, and the gap keeps closing. September 20, 2026.
excerpt: From a factory-floor supervisor now running a $27.9 billion company, to a diaspora quietly closing a billion-dollar philanthropy gap, September 20's five stories are about decisions and totals that were still moving when they were counted.
bodyHtml:
None of today's five people or institutions knew how their bet would turn out when they made it. That's what makes each one worth telling before the ending is obvious.

93% of India's rare earth magnets come from one country. Twenty companies just bid to change that.

Every EV motor and wind turbine needs a rare earth permanent magnet. In FY25, India imported 53,700 tonnes of them - 93% from China. In November 2025, India's Cabinet approved a Rs 7,280 crore scheme to build a domestic industry from scratch. By August 2026, 20 companies including L&T, Coal India and ReNew had submitted bids targeting 6,000 tonnes of annual production capacity. The winners haven't been picked yet - the outcome is still open.

He built India's first computer. His company now builds the machines that count its votes.

Dr. A. S. Rao, born September 20, 1914, founded the Electronics Corporation of India Limited in 1967 to build India's electronics and computing capability at a time when computers were entirely imported. Under his leadership, ECIL's TDC series became India's first indigenously designed and manufactured digital computers through the 1970s. Decades later, the same institution built the EVM and VVPAT machines used in Indian elections today - a direct line from one founder's mandate to the mechanics of the world's largest democracy.

From a factory floor to launching a company built for the AI boom

Revathi Advaithi began her career in an entry-level factory-floor supervisor role and rose to CEO of Flex Ltd., a $27.9 billion global manufacturing company. In May 2026, she announced she would lead a spin-off, Axiom Solutions International, built around Flex's power business for AI data centers - a segment that grew 38% year-over-year to $6.6 billion. Born and educated in India, her path ran through decades of hands-on operations work before landing her at the center of the global AI infrastructure race.

The diaspora doesn't just earn abroad - it's closing a billion-dollar giving gap

Indian American philanthropic giving reached an estimated $4-5 billion in 2024, nearly tripling since 2018, according to a joint report from Dalberg, Indiaspora and the India Philanthropy Alliance published October 30, 2025. The gap between what the community could give, based on its wealth, and what it actually gives has narrowed from $2-3 billion down to just $1 billion. The same report projects that if the next generation gives even 1% of an estimated $2 trillion in coming wealth transfer, annual giving could reach $20 billion - a projection, not a guarantee, but a direction the numbers are already moving in.

 

Doctors wanted to amputate. His family said no.

Sachin Sarjerao Khilari developed gangrene from a bicycle accident as a schoolboy. Doctors recommended amputation; his family refused. He became a mechanical engineer and a UPSC exam tutor, competed in javelin, and switched to shot put after a 2019 shoulder injury. At the Paris 2024 Paralympics, he won silver in the men's shot put F46 final with a 16.32-meter throw - an Asian record, and 0.06 meters from gold.

Five stories, one thread: a bid submitted before the winner is known, a machine built before its second purpose existed, a spin-off announced before the market proves it out, a giving gap narrowing before anyone declared it closed, a limb saved before anyone could promise what it would go on to do. Committing to an outcome you can't yet see is the harder version of confidence - and it's the version all five of today's stories actually required.

He built India's first digital computer. Decades later, he built the machine that counts India's votes.
Doctors wanted to amputate his leg as a schoolboy. His family said no - and he became a Paralympic silver medalist.
She started on a factory floor. She now runs a $27.9 billion company - and is about to spin off another.
